sense: where something is: in a place

evidence: Hor. C. 2.16.13–14: splendet in mēnsā tenuī salīnum
Vulg. Jo. 14.2: In domō Patris meī mānsiōnēs multae sunt
terms.comment: The ablative answers “where?” (ubi?); with the accusative in answers “where to?” and means into or onto (see into). English “in” and “on” are both in with the ablative: in urbe, in town; in mēnsā, on the table.

terms.gloss: at home, in the country; in Rome, in Corinth
evidence: Plin. NH 19.51: Rōmae quidem per sē hortus ager pauperis erat
Cic. Att. 13.49.1: quam equidem rūrī esse arbitror
terms.comment: Names of towns and small islands take no preposition: singular nouns of the first and second declensions stand in the locative (Rōmae, Corinthī), the rest in the ablative (Athēnīs, Carthāgine). So do domī, at home, rūrī, in the country, and humī, on the ground. Domī meae, at my house: see at the house of.

evidence: Ov. Met. 11.608–609: jānua … nūlla domō tōtā est
terms.comment: With locus (hōc locō, eōdem locō), and often with a noun that has tōtus (tōtā urbe), the preposition is left out.

phrases.latin: In domō Patris meī mānsiōnēs multae sunt.
phrases.english: In my Father’s house are many rooms.

phrases.latin: exāmen apum in arbore praetōriō imminente cōnsēderat
phrases.english: a swarm of bees had settled in a tree overhanging the general’s tent

phrases.latin: dōnāstī, Lupe, rūs sub urbe nōbīs; sed rūs est mihi majus in fenestrā
phrases.english: you have given me a farm outside town, Lupus; but I have a bigger farm in my window

phrases.latin: Rōmae quidem per sē hortus ager pauperis erat
phrases.english: at Rome the garden was in itself the poor man’s field

phrases.latin: Atticae prīmum salūtem (quam equidem rūrī esse arbitror; multam igitur salūtem)
phrases.english: first, greetings to Attica (who I think is in the country; so, many greetings)

phrases.latin: jānua nē versō strīdōrēs cardine reddat, nūlla domō tōtā est
phrases.english: so that no door may creak as its hinge turns, there is none in the whole house
